entries.text: Single Sprint Important Velocity Rules • Binary Counting: Story points are counted on an all-or-nothing basis. If an 8-point story is 90% complete at the end of a Sprint, it contributes 0 points to that Sprint's velocity. The item remains in the backlog, and points are counted only when it is fully completed in a future Sprint. • Team-Specific Metric: Velocity is a unique metric tied to a specific team's capacity, culture, and relative baseline. Velocity cannot be used to compare performance between different teams. A team delivering 50 points per Sprint is not inherently more productive than a team delivering 20 points, as their underlying point baselines differ. Forecasting Work with Mean Velocity Once a team establishes a stable historical baseline over 3 to 5 Sprints, velocity enables empirical forecasting: Where is the mean velocity across observed Sprints. If a Product Backlog contains 150 total Story Points and the team maintains a mean velocity ( ) of 25 points/Sprint, the expected remaining duration to release is calculated as: 3.5 Burndown Visual Analytics Visual tracking charts convert raw team performance data into clear, actionable progress indicators. entries.text: Product Backlog Refinement Activity Task Sheet Session Duration: 30–45 Minutes Team Structure: Groups of 6 Developers Your Role: Development Team (Software Engineers / UI Designers) Instructor Role: Product Owner (PO) 1. Project Brief: Campus Express (Food Delivery App) Campus Express is a mobile application designed for university students and staff to order meals from campus dining halls and local food vendors for fast delivery directly to dorms, libraries, or lecture halls. As the Product Owner (PO), I understand the business vision and user needs, but I rely on you—the Development Team—to evaluate technical feasibility, highlight implementation complexities, ask clarifying questions, and help determine the final release priority. 2. Session Objectives During this refinement session, your group will work through the initial Product Backlog to: 1. Clarify Requirements: Ask the PO questions to uncover missing edge cases or technical assumptions. 2. Estimate Relative Effort (Sizing): Assign Story Points using the Modified Fibonacci Sequence [1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 20, 40, 100] based on Complexity, Effort, and Risk/Uncertainty. 3. Decompose Large Items: If a story is too large or risky (typically >13 points), split it into smaller, manageable PBIs. 4. Advise on Priority: Help the PO adjust the backlog priority based on technical dependencies and effort vs. value tradeoffs. 3. Definition of Done (DoD) Reference Keep our baseline quality standard in mind when estimating effort: • [ ] UI wireframe sketched with interactive navigation flow. • [ ] Acceptance criteria fully satisfied. • [ ] Peer-reviewed by at least one other developer. • [ ] Verified integration with upstream/downstream screens.

entries.text: 5. Step-by-Step Instructions for Teams • Step 1: Read & Question (10 Mins) Review each story as a group. Formulate specific technical or business questions for the Product Owner (e.g., "Does Checkout need real-time credit card gateway integration or just campus card mockups?"). Raise your hand to ask the PO during the session. • Step 2: Relative Sizing (10 Mins) Run rapid Planning Poker within your team: o Pick US-01 or US-03 as your baseline reference task (e.g., 2 or 3 Story Points). o Vote on remaining items using cards [1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 20, 40, 100]. o If estimates diverge significantly, have the highest and lowest voters explain their technical reasoning, then re-vote until consensus is reached. • Step 3: Backlog Decompositions (10 Mins) Identify any story estimated at 13 points or higher. Split it into two or more smaller user stories (e.g., splitting US-06 Checkout & Payment into Delivery Location Selection and Payment Gateway Processing). • Step 4: Priority Alignment & Delivery (5 Mins) Re-order your refined backlog table based on technical dependencies (e.g., Menu Selection must precede Cart Summary) and communicate recommended priority adjustments to the PO.

entries.title: Requirements Engineering - Lecture Slides.pdf · p. 2
entries.text: CHAPTER 4 AGENDA Learning Objectives ● Explain why RE happens upfront in Waterfall, vs. continuously in Agile. ● Describe the 5 RE phases and the deliverable each one produces. ● Distinguish User Requirements from System Requirements — and avoid the “rabbit hole” trap. ● Write unambiguous requirements using the 5 EARS patterns, and write measurable Non-Functional Requirements. ● Classify requirements with FURPS+ and detect conflicts with an interaction grid. ● Structure a Software Requirements Specification (SRS), including use cases, tables, and UML. ● Apply the 5 validation checks and multiple validation techniques, individually and in combination. ● Explain traceability (RTM) and the Change Control Board (CCB) process. ● Apply all of the above to a running case study: a University Timetabling System. Chapter 4 — Requirements Engineering 2

entries.text: 4.1 WHERE THIS CHAPTER FITS From Agile Back to Waterfall In Chapter 3, we studied Agile: iterative development, flexible scope, continuous feedback, requirements that evolve sprint by sprint. Chapter 3 was the only chapter using Agile. From here on — Requirements Engineering, Design, Implementation, Testing — we operate inside the traditional Waterfall Model. Watch for this: the heavy documentation and formal sign-offs in this chapter exist because of Waterfall’s plan- driven nature — not because they're universally “the right way” to do RE. Chapter 4 — Requirements Engineering 3

Requirements 2. System Design 3. Implementation 4. Testing You are here No built-in reverse gear. Once a phase is signed off, there is no formal mechanism to revisit it — which is exactly why the Requirements phase you're about to learn is so rigorous: mistakes made here are the most expensive to fix later. entries.title: Requirements Engineering - Lecture Slides.pdf · p. 10
entries.text: 4.2.1 THE RE ROADMAP What Is Requirements Engineering? Requirements define what a system should do, plus the constraints it must operate under. Requirements Engineering (RE) is the process of discovering, analyzing, documenting, and validating those needs — five interlocking phases, each with its own deliverable (Sections 4.3–4.7): 1. Elicitation 0. Feasibility 2. Analysis 3. Specification 4. Validation → Elicitation → Feasibility Report → Organized Reqs → Draft SRS → Baselined SRS Register Not a rigid pipeline: Validation regularly sends work back to Elicitation or Analysis when gaps are found, and Specification draws directly on what Analysis has organized. Chapter 4 — Requirements Engineering 11

entries.title: Requirements Engineering - Lecture Slides.pdf · p. 11
entries.text: 4.2.2 THE SPIRAL VIEW Three Loops of Progressive Refinement The internal RE process is iterative: the same activities repeat at three increasing depths. Chapter 4 — Requirements Engineering 12

entries.title: Requirements Engineering - Lecture Slides.pdf · p. 12
entries.text: 4.2.2 THE SPIRAL VIEW Why the Direction Matters Business → User → System. Each loop's validated output becomes the input the next loop refines. Skipping straight to the System loop without validating Business and User needs first is one of the most common — and costly — mistakes in Waterfall RE. Chapter 4 — Requirements Engineering 13

entries.text: 4.4.3 USE CASE DIAGRAMS Use Case Diagrams: A First Map of Actors and Use Cases Before writing a detailed use case description, it helps to see the whole system at a glance — a lightweight sketch of who does what. Use Case Diagram. Groups system functions visually by user role (“Actors”) and by system boundary. It requires no analysis yet — it is simply a map of the raw material, not a judgment about it. Each oval — each candidate use case — becomes a target for a full Use Case Description next. The diagram scopes which interactions exist; the description spells out how one plays out, step by step. entries.text: 4.4.3 FREQUENTLY ASKED Should Use Case Descriptions Be Written in Stage 1 or Stage 3? Both — but for different purposes, at different levels of finish: Stage 1 (Elicitation): drafted informally, in the stakeholder's own language, focused on the happy path. Its job is to confirm the team correctly understood one specific interaction. Stage 3 (Specification): the same use case is revisited, finalized, and formalized — every extension and alternate flow is fully specified, and it becomes part of the baselined SRS (Section 4.6.1). Chapter 4 — Requirements Engineering 28

entries.title: Requirements Engineering - Lecture Slides.pdf · p. 28
entries.text: 4.4.5 OUTPUT OF ELICITATION Output of the Elicitation Phase Elicitation ends when the team has captured a broad, honest picture of stakeholder needs — not a tidy one. Nothing below is yet classified, prioritized, or checked for conflicts. Deliverable Description Elicitation Register The running log of raw, informally-tagged requirement statements. A lightweight actor/system-boundary sketch scoping which interactions exist — not Draft Use Case Diagram yet analyzed. Draft Use Case Descriptions Happy-path-only narratives confirming the team's understanding of key interactions. Who was consulted, and which Viewpoint they represent (formalized as VOA in Stakeholder & Viewpoint List Phase 2, Section 4.5.2). Domain Glossary (Draft) A first pass at shared terminology, to be refined as Analysis proceeds. Supporting Artifacts Interview notes, workshop minutes, field observations, low-fidelity prototypes. Chapter 4 — Requirements Engineering 30

entries.title: Requirements Engineering - Lecture Slides.pdf · p. 29
entries.text: CASE STUDY CHECKPOINT Elicitation: Three Stakeholders, Three Raw Statements The team runs interviews and a workshop with Sarah (a Student), Dr. Li (a Lecturer), and Ms. Lee (the Facility Administrator). The Elicitation Register fills up: E-001 (Sarah): “I want to see my class schedule on my phone, not just on the desktop portal.” E-002 (Dr. Li): “When I need to swap a room urgently, right now I have to email the admin and hope she sees it in time.” E-003 (Ms. Lee): “Room swaps should never bypass my sign-off — I'm accountable for room conflicts.” These raw, unorganized entries — plus a draft Use Case (UC-04, from E-002) — move to Phase 2 for analysis. Chapter 4 — Requirements Engineering 31

entries.title: Requirements Engineering - Lecture Slides.pdf · p. 30
entries.text: Phase 2: Requirements Analysis & 4.5 Classification Turning a raw pile of requests into a structured framework Chapter 4 — Requirements Engineering 32

entries.title: Requirements Engineering - Lecture Slides.pdf · p. 31
entries.text: 4.5.0 WHAT IS ANALYSIS & CLASSIFICATION? From Raw Statements to a Structured Foundation Requirements Analysis & Classification takes the raw, unfiltered Elicitation Register and turns it into a structured, unambiguous foundation for Specification. It has two jobs — and neither one is capturing new facts, which is Elicitation's job: 1. Organize 2. Classify Sort each raw statement into User Requirements Rewrite each statement in EARS syntax (Section 4.5.2) (what stakeholders need) vs. System Requirements so it says one thing only, tag it under FURPS+ (Section (how it will be built), and check every viewpoint is 4.5.3), and check it against every other requirement represented (Section 4.5.1, VOA). for hidden conflicts (Section 4.5.4). Input → Output. In: the raw Elicitation Register (Section 4.4.3). Out: an organized, EARS-formatted, conflict- checked requirement set — ready to be written into the formal SRS in Phase 3 (Specification). Chapter 4 — Requirements Engineering 33

entries.title: Requirements Engineering - Lecture Slides.pdf · p. 32
entries.text: 4.5.1 ORGANIZING REQUIREMENTS User Requirements vs. System Requirements User Requirements System Requirements Written for Stakeholders (non-technical) Developers and testers Style Natural language, simple tables, diagrams Structured, technical, precise What services does the user need? What are What exact functions, API endpoints, data Answers the business goals? structures, and constraints must exist? Why this distinction matters. User Requirements keep the SRS in language every stakeholder can validate and sign off on; System Requirements give developers and testers the precision to build and verify. Blur the two and either stakeholders can't confirm you understood them, or developers are left guessing — which is exactly how the “rabbit hole” trap (next slide) happens. Chapter 4 — Requirements Engineering 39

entries.title: Requirements Engineering - Lecture Slides.pdf · p. 33
entries.text: 4.5.1 ORGANIZING REQUIREMENTS Avoid the “Rabbit Hole” Trap Novice engineers often dive into low-level System Requirements — database schemas, API protocols, caching — before fully understanding the high-level User Requirements. This builds a well-engineered system that solves the wrong problem. Rule of thumb: you cannot specify how a system should work until you fully understand what problem the user is trying to solve. Chapter 4 — Requirements Engineering 40

entries.title: Requirements Engineering - Lecture Slides.pdf · p. 34
entries.text: 4.5.1 ORGANIZING REQUIREMENTS Viewpoint-Oriented Analysis (VOA) Purpose: VOA groups requirements by the perspective they come from, so analysis works through each perspective in turn instead of one undifferentiated pile: INTERACTOR INDIRECT DOMAIN Direct Users Indirect Stakeholders Domain Constraints People who directly interact with Never touch the system, but rely Environmental and technical the UI. on its outputs (auditors, limits imposed by the domain executives). itself. Why we need it. Requirements gathered from only one viewpoint — usually Direct Users — systematically miss Indirect Stakeholders' needs and Domain Constraints, exactly the kind of gap that surfaces expensively during Validation, or worse, after deployment. Checking all three viewpoints before Specification is what makes the analysis complete, not just plausible. Chapter 4 — Requirements Engineering 41

entries.title: Requirements Engineering - Lecture Slides.pdf · p. 35
entries.text: 4.5.2 FORMALIZING WITH EARS EARS: Easy Approach to Requirements Syntax Before the raw Elicitation Register can be organized, classified, or checked for conflicts, every entry needs one fixed sentence template — so two readers can no longer interpret the same requirement two different ways. Five patterns cover every case: 1 Ubiquitous The <system> shall <response>. Always true WHEN <trigger>, the <system> shall 2 Event-Driven A specific event fires it <response>. WHILE <in state>, the <system> shall 3 State-Driven Only during a state <response>. WHERE <feature included>, the <system> 4 Option-Driven Optional feature/config shall <response>. IF <error>, THEN the <system> shall 5 Unwanted Behavior Error handling <response>. Chapter 4 — Requirements Engineering 34

entries.title: Requirements Engineering - Lecture Slides.pdf · p. 39
entries.text: 4.5.2 EARS PATTERNS EARS Quick Reference Pattern Keyword Template Ubiquitous (none) The <system> shall <response>. Event-Driven WHEN WHEN <trigger>, the <system> shall <response>. State-Driven WHILE WHILE <in state>, the <system> shall <response>. Option-Driven WHERE WHERE <feature included>, the <system> shall <response>. Unwanted Behavior IF ... THEN IF <error/trigger>, THEN the <system> shall <response>. Why this comes before Organizing and Classifying. A requirement in EARS form has its trigger, condition, and response as separate, identifiable parts — exactly what's needed to tag it under FURPS+ and to compare it against others in a conflict-detection grid. Chapter 4 — Requirements Engineering 38

entries.title: Requirements Engineering - Lecture Slides.pdf · p. 40
entries.text: 4.5.3 FR & NFR IN DEPTH Functional Requirements, by Category Functional Requirements (FR) define a specific behavior the system must perform. They answer “what does the system do?” and are written using the EARS patterns you learned in Section 4.5.2. Category Example Functional Requirement WHEN a student updates their profile address, the system shall update the central student Data Management information database. User Management The system shall allow an administrator to deactivate a lecturer account. Reporting The system shall generate a weekly room-utilization report grouped by department. WHEN a new semester is created, the system shall synchronize course codes with the Integration university's ERP system. Chapter 4 — Requirements Engineering 52

entries.title: Requirements Engineering - Lecture Slides.pdf · p. 41
entries.text: 4.5.3 FR & NFR IN DEPTH Writing Measurable Non-Functional Requirements Non-Functional Requirements (NFR) define a quality attribute — not what the system does, but how well. An NFR is only useful if a tester can look at it and say Pass or Fail with no argument. The <system> shall <behavior> within/under <threshold + unit> when/under <condition>. Metric Threshold Condition What is being measured (time, A specific number with a unit. The context under which the throughput, error rate, uptime %, “Fast” is not a threshold; “2 threshold applies (load level, concurrent users). seconds” is. network type, hardware). entries.text: 4.5.3 FR & NFR IN DEPTH From Vague to Measurable Vague (Unmeasurable) Rewritten (Measurable) “The system shall return search results within 2 seconds for 95% of queries “The system shall be fast.” under normal load (≤100 concurrent users).” “A first-time user shall complete the room-swap workflow in under 3 “The system shall be user-friendly.” minutes without external help.” “The system shall encrypt all data at rest using AES-256 and require multi- “The system shall be secure.” factor authentication for admins.” “The system shall maintain 99.9% uptime measured monthly, excluding “The system shall be reliable.” scheduled maintenance.” Chapter 4 — Requirements Engineering 54

entries.title: Requirements Engineering - Lecture Slides.pdf · p. 43
entries.text: 4.5.3 CHALLENGE: FR VS. NFR BLENDING Resolution — the FURPS+ Framework Stakeholders rarely separate the two on their own. Engineers are expected to identify FR apart from NFR. — FURPS+ gives six categories to sort them into: F Functionality U Usability R Reliability Features, capabilities, Human factors, Availability, accuracy, security aesthetics, docs recoverability P Performance S Supportability + Constraints Speed, throughput, Testability, maintainability Design, Implementation, response time Interface, Physical Example: “The system shall print invoices instantly” splits into a Functional req. (support printing) + a Performance req. (completes within 2 seconds). Chapter 4 — Requirements Engineering 42

entries.title: Requirements Engineering - Lecture Slides.pdf · p. 44
entries.text: 4.5.3 FREQUENTLY ASKED Is the “F” in FURPS+ the Same as a Functional Requirement (FR)? No —It is not a true Functional Requirement. ”F” in FURPS+ (Functionality) is a category — feature set, security scope, audit and compliance controls — used to group and review related requirements together. It is a label, not a testable sentence. FR (Functional Requirement) is one individual, EARS-formatted, testable statement (Section 4.6.3) Why put an F in an NFR-style framework? They describe a quality of a function, not the function itself. But got grouped under "F" because they don't fit neatly under Usability, Reliability, Performance, or Supportability either. Chapter 4 — Requirements Engineering 43

entries.title: Requirements Engineering - Lecture Slides.pdf · p. 45
entries.text: THE SIMPLE TEST One Question Separates Them Can I remove this requirement and the system still does the same task, just less safely, traceably, or controllably? NO — THE TASK DISAPPEARS YES — THE TASK STILL WORKS → It’s a true FR → It sits under “F” Write it as an EARS statement and attach it Document it once as a cross-cutting review item, directly to the feature's acceptance criteria. referenced by every feature it touches. Example: “The system shall allow a user to cancel Example: “All trading actions require MFA” or a pending order before execution.” “every trade generates an immutable audit log entry.” FURPS+ Quick Reference — FR vs. “F” 3

entries.title: Requirements Engineering - Lecture Slides.pdf · p. 46
entries.text: SIDE-BY-SIDE · TRADING SYSTEM EXAMPLES FR or “F”? A Working Example Requirement Type Why The system shall allow a user to place a limit order FR Removing it deletes a feature. specifying price and quantity. The system shall allow a user to cancel a pending order FR A discrete, testable action. before execution. Order placement still works — just The system shall encrypt all API traffic using TLS 1.2+. “F” insecurely — without it. The system shall log every trade with timestamp, user ID, Adds traceability; doesn’t change what “F” and order details. the trade does. Rule of thumb: if the rule is core business logic tied to one feature, write it as an FR inside that feature. If it’s a cross- cutting policy applied across many features, document it once under “F.” FURPS+ Quick Reference — FR vs. “F” 4

entries.title: Requirements Engineering - Lecture Slides.pdf · p. 47
entries.text: 4.5.4 CHALLENGE: HIDDEN CONFLICTS Resolution — Matrix-Based Interaction Analysis An architectural conflict occurs when satisfying one requirement makes another harder to satisfy (e.g., real-time speed vs. heavy encryption). Score every pair: +1 Compatible, 0 Neutral, −1 Conflict. FR1: Mobile NFR1: Load < 3s NFR2: Encryption FR2: Swap FR1: Mobile — +1 0 0 NFR1: Load < 3s +1 — −1 (Conflict) 0 NFR2: Encryption 0 −1 (Conflict) — 0 FR2: Swap 0 0 0 — Reading it: NFR1 and NFR2 conflict — encryption overhead works against the load-time budget, an explicit trade-off is needed before any code is written. Note: tags like “NFR1” are shorthand for the full EARS statement written in Section 4.5.1 — the grid only works because each requirement is already precise enough to compare. entries.text: 4.6.0 WHAT IS SPECIFICATION? From Organized Requirements to a Baselined SRS Requirements Specification takes the organized, classified requirements from Phase 2 and writes them into one authoritative, contractually-binding document: the Software Requirements Specification (SRS). Once the Joint Steering Committee signs it, the SRS becomes the baseline every later phase is measured against. From User to System One Document, Every Artifact Governed, Not Casual Every User Requirement (UR) is EARS-formatted FRs, measurable A dedicated sign-off process and refined into one or more precise NFRs, use cases, and UML two recurring failure modes — System Requirements (SR) — see diagrams are all assembled into ambiguity and over-specification the worked UR → SR examples the standard SRS structure, next. — are guarded against before ahead. baselining. entries.title: Requirements Engineering - Lecture Slides.pdf · p. 50
entries.text: 4.6.1 THE SRS DOCUMENT Standard SRS Structure Every artifact this chapter has built — requirements, EARS statements, use cases, the interaction grid — is ultimately assembled into one document: the Software Requirements Specification (SRS). Section Contents 1. Introduction Purpose, scope, definitions/glossary, references, document overview. 2. Overall Description Product perspective, product functions summary, user characteristics, constraints. 3.1 FR (EARS syntax) · 3.2 External Interfaces · 3.3 NFR (FURPS+, measurable) · 3.4 Use 3. Specific Requirements Cases & UML. Data dictionary, Requirements Traceability Matrix, interaction analysis grid, revision 4. Appendices history. 5. Approval / Sign-off Signatures from the Joint Steering Committee, marking the document baselined. Chapter 4 — Requirements Engineering 48

entries.text: Requirements Traceability & Change 4.8 Control Protecting the baselined SRS from unmanaged scope creep Chapter 4 — Requirements Engineering 64

entries.title: Requirements Engineering - Lecture Slides.pdf · p. 62
entries.text: 4.8.1 TRACEABILITY Forward, Backward, and Bidirectional Type Direction Purpose Connects user requirements down to specs, code, and tests — Bidirectional Both ways and back. Every requirement is designed, coded, tested. Prevents “omitted Forward Requirement → Code/Test scope.” Every piece of code maps to an authorized requirement. Prevents Backward Code/Test → Requirement “Gold Plating.” What is “Gold Plating”? Building unrequested features or unnecessary complexity — “while I'm in here, I'll also add…” It inflates cost and schedule without adding contracted value. Backward traceability is the main defense: if code doesn't map to a requirement ID, it shouldn't exist. Chapter 4 — Requirements Engineering 65

THE CCB EVALUATES EVERY CHANGE FROM FOUR ANGLES Lead System Project Sponsor Project Manager QA Manager Architect Business necessity; Impact on schedule, Technical feasibility, Re-testing effort, approves financial cost milestones, staffing. refactoring complexity. regression risk. additions. entries.title: Requirements Engineering - Lecture Slides.pdf · p. 68
entries.text: CASE STUDY CHECKPOINT Traceability & Change Control: A Real ECR Six months after baselining, a new data-privacy regulation requires all schedule data in transit to be encrypted end-to-end — the risk the Interaction Grid had only flagged as “future” back in Analysis. A Facility IT lead submits an ECR. The ECR writes the anticipated risk into a real requirement for the first time: NFR2 — “The system shall encrypt all schedule and swap-request data in transit using TLS 1.3, and at rest using AES-256.” The team consults the RTM: the change touches SR-1.1 and its test case TC-API-204 will need updating, since encryption overhead affects the 3.0s load-time budget — precisely the NFR1-vs-NFR2 trade-off logged during Analysis. The CCB approves it — the SRS is re-baselined as v1.1, and the RTM rows for SR-1.1 and the new NFR2 are updated. Chapter 4 — Requirements Engineering 71

entries.title: Requirements Engineering - Lecture Slides.pdf · p. 69
entries.text: QUICK REFERENCE Telling the ID Codes Apart Several ID prefixes appear side by side in this chapter — here's how to tell them apart: Prefix Meaning Assigned During Example E-xxx Raw statement from Elicitation, unanalyzed. Phase 1 (Elicitation) E-002 UC-xx Use Case: an actor–system interaction. Phase 1 → Phase 3 UC-04 UR-x User Requirement — organized, for stakeholders. Phase 2 (Analysis) UR-2 SR-x.x System Requirement — technical, from one UR. Phase 3 (Specification) SR-2.1 FRx / NFRx Functional / Non-Functional Requirement (SRS's list). Phase 3 (Specification) FR1, NFR1 TC-xxx Test Case — verifies one requirement (in the RTM). Phase 4 (Validation) TC-API-204 Reading the numbering. SR-2.1 means “the 1st System Requirement derived from UR-2” — the decimal ties it to its parent UR. FR/NFR numbers, by contrast, just count sequentially through the SRS's formal requirement list; they don't encode a parent ID. Chapter 4 — Requirements Engineering 73

entries.text: PHASE 4 · CASE STUDY CHECKPOINT A Validation Walkthrough Catches a Conflict During a walkthrough with Dr. Li and Ms. Lee, a reviewer places UR-2 (urgent swap) and UR-4 (FIFO waitlist) side by side and asks a simple question: “if an urgent swap and a routine waitlist request target the same room, which one wins?” Neither requirement says. The gap is logged as a Validation finding, not silently patched — it goes back to Specification for a fix: SR-4.1 is revised to add an explicit exception — “WHERE the incoming request is flagged urgent per UC-04, the system shall place it ahead of the FIFO waitlist, subject to Ms. Lee's sign-off per UR-2.” This is exactly why Validation is a separate phase from Specification: it's what catches a contradiction between two individually reasonable requirements before either one gets built. Elicitation captured them, Analysis organized and classified them, Specification made them precise and testable, Validation caught the one contradiction that would have shipped a broken waitlist, and Traceability now ties every one of them to a design module and a test case in a single governed document. That is what “doing Requirements Engineering” actually produces — not a slide deck, but this. Chapter 4 Supplement — Elicitation Artifacts 28

entries.title: Week 5 Lecture.pdf · p. 3
entries.text: 1 What Is System Modeling? Why engineers draw pictures of systems before they build them System Modeling with UML 2

entries.title: Week 5 Lecture.pdf · p. 4
entries.text: FOUNDATIONS Why We Model • Real systems are huge — nobody can hold all the detail in their head at once. • Most failed projects fail for three ordinary reasons: misunderstood requirements, problems found too late, or excess complexity. • A model deliberately leaves out detail so one aspect — context, structure, behaviour — is easy to discuss. • Since the 1990s, UML has been the standard notation family for these pictures. System Modeling with UML 3

entries.title: Week 5 Lecture.pdf · p. 5
entries.text: FOUNDATIONS Existing System vs. Planned System Existing system Planned (new) system Model-driven engineering A requirements-engineering A design activity. Explains a The model isn't just activity. Clarifies what the proposed design, argues about documentation — some tool current system does and gives alternatives, and documents it chains generate an a shared basis for discussion. well enough to build. implementation directly from it. System Modeling with UML 4

entries.title: Week 5 Lecture.pdf · p. 6
entries.text: FOUNDATIONS Four Perspectives on One System Perspective The question it answers Diagrams used External / context What lies outside my system? Context diagrams Interaction How do people and systems interact? Use case, sequence Structural How is the system's data structured? Class diagrams Behavioural How does the system change over time? Activity, state machine System Modeling with UML 5

entries.title: Week 5 Lecture.pdf · p. 7
entries.text: FOUNDATIONS How Precise Does a Model Need to Be? • As a discussion tool — incomplete or slightly incorrect is fine; its job is to support conversation. • As documentation of an existing system — must be accurate, but can still leave out irrelevant parts. • As a specification for code generation — must be correct and complete; a machine acts on it directly. • Before you draw anything: who is this diagram for, and what decision are they trying to reach? System Modeling with UML 6

entries.title: Week 5 Lecture.pdf · p. 8
entries.text: 2 Context Models What lies outside the system we're building? System Modeling with UML 7

entries.title: Week 5 Lecture.pdf · p. 9
entries.text: CONTEXT MODELS Reading a Context Diagram • Draws a boundary and shows only the other systems it touches. • Says nothing about how the system is used, or what's inside it. • Where the boundary sits is “a political judgment” — not purely technical. • Usually paired with an activity diagram of the surrounding process. System Modeling with UML 8

entries.title: Week 5 Lecture.pdf · p. 10
entries.text: 3 Interaction Models I Use Case Diagrams System Modeling with UML 9

entries.title: Week 5 Lecture.pdf · p. 11
entries.text: USE CASE DIAGRAMS The Anatomy of a Use Case Diagram A use case diagram is a high-level picture of what a system does and who interacts with it. It captures the system's functional requirements from the user's point of view, without showing internal design, data structures, or the order in which things happen. A use case in a use case diagram is a specific goal that an actor achieves by interacting with the system. • System boundary — rectangle naming the system. • Actor — a role, not a person; a stick figure outside the boundary. • Use case — an oval named with a verb phrase. • Association — a plain line, actor to use case. System Modeling with UML 10

entries.title: Week 5 Lecture.pdf · p. 12
entries.text: USE CASE DIAGRAMS Actors, in More Depth • An actor is anything external that produces or consumes data at the boundary — person, system, device, even a timer. • Primary — a user whose goal the use case exists to fulfil. • Supporting — provides a service to the use case (e.g. a payment processor). • Offstage — has a stake in the outcome without using the system directly (e.g. a regulator). System Modeling with UML 11

entries.title: Week 5 Lecture.pdf · p. 13
entries.text: USE CASE DIAGRAMS Include, Extend & Generalization • «include» — always happens; arrow points to the included use case. • «extend» — optional; arrow points back to the base use case. • Generalization — a child use case inherits a parent's behaviour. • Rule of thumb: include is “I always need this”; extend is “I might add this.” System Modeling with UML 12

entries.title: Week 5 Lecture.pdf · p. 14
entries.text: USE CASE DIAGRAMS A Checklist for a Clean Diagram • Identify the boundary first, and name it clearly. • Show actors as roles, outside the boundary. • Name use cases as goals, with a verb phrase. • «include» mandatory behaviour; «extend» optional behaviour. • Use generalization sparingly. System Modeling with UML 13

entries.title: Week 5 Lecture.pdf · p. 15
entries.text: USE CASE DIAGRAMS Worked Example: Requirements First, Then the Diagram • A real requirements engineer starts from what the customer says, not from a blank canvas. • EARS (Easy Approach to Requirements Syntax) writes that down in a few fixed sentence shapes, so nothing stays ambiguous. • The rest of this worked example — diagram, fully-dressed description, sequence diagram — is all derived from the same requirements set. System Modeling with UML 14

entries.title: Week 5 Lecture.pdf · p. 16
entries.text: USE CASE DIAGRAMS Requirements First: EARS Format Pattern Shape Ubiquitous The <system> shall <response>. Event-driven WHEN <trigger>, the <system> shall <response>. State-driven WHILE <state>, the <system> shall <response>. Unwanted behaviour IF <condition>, THEN the <system> shall <response>. A combination, e.g. WHILE <state> IF <condition> THEN the <system> shall Complex <response>. System Modeling with UML 15

entries.title: Week 5 Lecture.pdf · p. 17
entries.text: USE CASE DIAGRAMS Requirements Collected from the Customer (excerpt) • OBS-01 (Ubiquitous): The system shall require login before any account function. • OBS-06 (Event-driven): WHEN a customer selects “Transfer Funds”, the system shall display eligible accounts. • OBS-08 (Unwanted): IF the amount exceeds the balance, THEN the system shall show insufficient-funds and stop. • OBS-14 (State-driven): WHILE the confirmation screen is shown, the system shall allow cancel instead of confirm. Full set (OBS-01 – OBS-20) is in the use case description example PDF. System Modeling with UML 16

entries.title: Week 5 Lecture.pdf · p. 18
entries.text: USE CASE DIAGRAMS From Requirements to the Diagram Use Case Actor Source Requirements Login Customer OBS-01, 02, 03, 04 View Account Balance Customer OBS-05 Transfer Funds Customer OBS-06 – 14 Pay Bills Customer OBS-15 Logout Customer OBS-16, 17 Manage Customer Accounts Bank Administrator OBS-18, 19 Generate Reports Bank Administrator OBS-18, 20 System Modeling with UML 17

entries.title: Week 5 Lecture.pdf · p. 19
entries.text: USE CASE DIAGRAMS Worked Example — Online Banking System Reconstructed directly from the EARS requirements above, not invented from scratch. System Modeling with UML 18

entries.title: Week 5 Lecture.pdf · p. 20
entries.text: USE CASE DIAGRAMS Use Case Description Check out the use case description example PDF Field What it captures Use case / Primary actor The use case's name, and the actor whose goal drives it. Preconditions What must already be true before the use case can start. Main flow The numbered happy-path steps, in order. Labelled by the step they branch from (e.g. “4a”) — a different, still-valid Alternate flow(s) path. Exception flow(s) Labelled the same way — caused by a fault, not a user choice. Postconditions What must be true once the use case ends, for both success and failure. System Modeling with UML 19

entries.title: Week 5 Lecture.pdf · p. 21
entries.text: USE CASE DIAGRAMS Worked Example — Transfer Funds: Main Flow 1. Customer selects “Transfer Funds” from the account menu. [OBS-06] 2. System displays the customer's eligible accounts. [OBS-06] 3. Customer selects a source account, destination account, and amount. [OBS-07] 4. System validates the amount and the destination account. [OBS-07] 5. System displays a confirmation screen. [OBS-10] 6. Customer confirms the transfer. [OBS-11] 7. System debits, credits, and generates a reference number. [OBS-11] 8. System displays a transfer receipt and records the transaction. [OBS-13] System Modeling with UML 20

entries.title: Week 5 Lecture.pdf · p. 22
entries.text: USE CASE DIAGRAMS Transfer Funds — Alternate & Exception Flows Ref At step Condition System response Insufficient-funds message; return to 4a 4 Insufficient funds. step 3. [OBS-08] Invalid-account message; return to 4b 4 Invalid destination account. step 3. [OBS-09] Discard transfer; return to Account 6a 6 Customer cancels. Summary. [OBS-14] Roll back; transfer-failed message; 7a (exception) 7 System/network fault while posting. keep reference. [OBS-12] System Modeling with UML 21

entries.title: Week 5 Lecture.pdf · p. 23
entries.text: 4 Interaction Models II Sequence Diagrams System Modeling with UML 22

entries.title: Week 5 Lecture.pdf · p. 24
entries.text: SEQUENCE DIAGRAMS The Anatomy of a Sequence Diagram A sequence diagram shows how parts of a system communicate and work together over time in sequence to accomplish one specific task. • Participants — shown as boxes along the top. An actor such as a human role or an external system, drawn as a stick figure. An object or component, drawn as a rectangle • Lifeline — a participant's timeline; time runs downward. • Activation bar — participant actively executing or waiting. • Synchronous message — show how participants communicate. Solid arrow, filled head, caller waits. • Return message — dashed arrow, response to synchronous message. System Modeling with UML 23

entries.title: Week 5 Lecture.pdf · p. 25
entries.text: SEQUENCE DIAGRAMS Grouping Behaviour with Frames/Fragments • alt — alternatives (if/else); each branch carries its own guard. • opt — an optional block; runs only if its one guard holds. • loop — the enclosed messages repeat per the guard condition. System Modeling with UML 24

entries.title: Week 5 Lecture.pdf · p. 26
entries.text: SEQUENCE DIAGRAMS Drawing a Sequence Diagram • Pick one scenario - Name it concretely, like "user places an order successfully" or "payment is declined”. Draw separate diagrams for the happy path and for important error cases, if draw them in one diagram becoming complex. • Decide level of detail - Keep the level consistent across the diagram. Mixing "Payment Gateway" with "StringUtils" in one picture makes it hard to read. • List the participants - Write down everyone involved in the scenario and place them left to right, roughly in the order they first take part. The initiator, usually an actor, goes on the far left. From left to right System Modeling with UML 24

entries.title: Week 5 Lecture.pdf · p. 27
entries.text: SEQUENCE DIAGRAMS Drawing a Sequence Diagram • Add messages in order - Start with the triggering message, then add each call and its response going down the page. For each one, decide whether it's sync or async, and label it with a method or action name plus key arguments, like save(order) • Add activation bars - Show when each participant is busy, nesting calls inside the bar of the caller that's waiting on them. System Modeling with UML 24

entries.title: Week 5 Lecture.pdf · p. 28
entries.text: SEQUENCE DIAGRAMS Drawing a Sequence Diagram • Add logic only where it matters - Use alt, opt, or loop fragments for branches or repetition that are important to the scenario. If the fragments start piling up, split the scenario into separate diagrams instead. System Modeling with UML 24

entries.title: Week 5 Lecture.pdf · p. 29
entries.text: SEQUENCE DIAGRAMS Scenario — User Login • A user opens the login page, enters a username and password, and submits the form. • The browser sends the credentials to an authentication server, which checks them against its records. • If valid, the server tells the browser to show a welcome message; if invalid, an error message instead. • Task: identify the participants, the message order, and how to represent the two outcomes. System Modeling with UML 25

entries.title: Week 5 Lecture.pdf · p. 30
entries.text: SEQUENCE DIAGRAMS Worked Example — User Login • Browser forwards credentials to the auth server. • Server checks them and reports success or failure. • alt: [login successful] vs. [login failed] branches. The alt frame makes the mutually exclusive outcomes of authResult() explicit. System Modeling with UML 26

entries.title: Week 5 Lecture.pdf · p. 31
entries.text: SEQUENCE DIAGRAMS Scenario — Online Shopping Checkout • A customer clicks Checkout; the web application shows an order summary and asks for shipping details. • The application forwards the order and amount to a payment gateway, which reports back success or failure. • Only if payment succeeded does the application update stock via an inventory system, then confirm the order. • Task: which combined fragment fits “only if — no explicit else”? It isn't the same one as Login. System Modeling with UML 27

entries.title: Week 5 Lecture.pdf · p. 32
entries.text: SEQUENCE DIAGRAMS Worked Example — Online Shopping Checkout System Modeling with UML 28

entries.title: Week 5 Lecture.pdf · p. 33
entries.text: SEQUENCE DIAGRAMS Scenario — Transfer Funds • An authenticated customer selects Transfer Funds, picks a source/destination account and amount, and submits. • The system validates: insufficient funds or an invalid destination account both stop the transfer with a message. • If valid, the system shows a confirmation screen and asks the customer to confirm or cancel. • Confirming posts the transfer via an account-ledger component; a posting fault rolls back, success shows a receipt. • Task: you will need more than one combined fragment — and one nested inside another. System Modeling with UML 29

entries.title: Week 5 Lecture.pdf · p. 34
entries.text: SEQUENCE DIAGRAMS Fragment Escalation: alt → opt → alt Requirement text Becomes… Traces to Three mutually exclusive validation Outer alt: [insufficient funds] / [invalid OBS-08/09/10 outcomes destination] / [valid]. Cancel → nothing further vs. confirm → opt nested in [valid], guard [customer OBS-14 post transfer, no explicit else confirms]. Posting fails vs. posting succeeds alt nested inside that opt. OBS-11/13 vs. 12 System Modeling with UML 30

entries.title: Week 5 Lecture.pdf · p. 35
entries.text: SEQUENCE DIAGRAMS Worked Example — Online Banking: Transfer Funds • Outer alt: the three validation outcomes. • Nested opt: customer confirms (else: nothing). • Nested alt: posting succeeds vs. posting fault. • Same escalation as Login → Checkout, just composed. System Modeling with UML 31

entries.text: SOFTWARE ENGINEERING · CHAPTER 4 Requirements Engineering Eliciting, analyzing, specifying, and validating what a system must do COURSE ROADMAP Chapter 1 Introduction to Software Engineering Chapter 2 The Software Process Chapter 3 Introduction to Agile Methodologies Chapter 4 Requirements Engineering (this chapter)

entries.title: Requirements Engineering - Lecture Slides ver 1.1.pdf · p. 2
entries.text: CHAPTER 4 AGENDA Learning Objectives ● Explain why RE happens upfront in Waterfall, vs. continuously in Agile. ● Describe the 5 RE phases and the deliverable each one produces. ● Distinguish User Requirements from System Requirements — and avoid the “rabbit hole” trap. ● Write unambiguous requirements using the 5 EARS patterns, and write measurable Non-Functional Requirements. ● Classify requirements with FURPS+ and detect conflicts with an interaction grid. ● Structure a Software Requirements Specification (SRS), including use cases, tables, and UML. ● Apply the 5 validation checks and multiple validation techniques, individually and in combination. ● Explain traceability (RTM) and the Change Control Board (CCB) process. ● Apply all of the above to a running case study: a University Timetabling System. Chapter 4 — Requirements Engineering 2

entries.title: Requirements Engineering - Lecture Slides ver 1.1.pdf · p. 3
entries.text: 4.1 WHERE THIS CHAPTER FITS From Agile Back to Waterfall In Chapter 3, we studied Agile: iterative development, flexible scope, continuous feedback, requirements that evolve sprint by sprint. Chapter 3 was the only chapter using Agile. From here on — Requirements Engineering, Design, Implementation, Testing — we operate inside the traditional Waterfall Model. Watch for this: the heavy documentation and formal sign-offs in this chapter exist because of Waterfall’s plan- driven nature — not because they're universally “the right way” to do RE. Chapter 4 — Requirements Engineering 3

entries.title: Requirements Engineering - Lecture Slides ver 1.1.pdf · p. 4
entries.text: 4.1 PROCESS FOUNDATIONS The Waterfall Model A sequential, plan-driven process. Each phase must be completed, reviewed, and formally approved before the next one begins. 1. Requirements 2. System Design 3. Implementation 4. Testing You are here No built-in reverse gear. Once a phase is signed off, there is no formal mechanism to revisit it — which is exactly why the Requirements phase you're about to learn is so rigorous: mistakes made here are the most expensive to fix later. Chapter 4 — Requirements Engineering 4

Both — but for different purposes, at different levels of finish: Stage 1 (Elicitation): drafted informally, in the stakeholder's own language, focused on the happy path. entries.text: 4.5.0 WHAT IS ANALYSIS & CLASSIFICATION? From Raw Statements to a Structured Foundation Requirements Analysis & Classification takes the raw, unfiltered Elicitation Register and turns it into a structured, unambiguous foundation for Specification. It has two jobs — and neither one is capturing new facts, which is Elicitation's job: 1. Organize 2. Classify Sort each raw statement into User Requirements Using the statement in EARS syntax (Section 4.5.1) so (what stakeholders need) vs. System Requirements it says one thing only, tag it under FURPS+ (Section (how it will be built), and check every viewpoint is 4.5.3), and check it against every other requirement represented (Section 4.5.2, VOA). for hidden conflicts (Section 4.5.4). Input → Output. In: the raw Elicitation Register (Section 4.4.3). Out: an organized, EARS-formatted, conflict- checked requirement set — ready to be written into the formal SRS in Phase 3 (Specification). Chapter 4 — Requirements Engineering 33

entries.text: 4.5.1 FORMALIZING WITH EARS EARS: Easy Approach to Requirements Syntax Before the raw Elicitation Register can be organized, classified, or checked for conflicts, every entry needs one fixed sentence template — so two readers can no longer interpret the same requirement two different ways. Five patterns cover every case: 1 Ubiquitous The <system> shall <response>. Always true WHEN <trigger>, the <system> shall 2 Event-Driven A specific event fires it <response>. WHILE <in state>, the <system> shall 3 State-Driven Only during a state <response>. WHERE <feature included>, the <system> 4 Option-Driven Optional feature/config shall <response>. IF <error>, THEN the <system> shall 5 Unwanted Behavior Error handling <response>. Chapter 4 — Requirements Engineering 34

State-Driven WHILE WHILE <in state>, the <system> shall <response>. Option-Driven WHERE WHERE <feature included>, the <system> shall <response>. Unwanted Behavior IF ... THEN IF <error/trigger>, THEN the <system> shall <response>. Why this comes before Organizing and Classifying. A requirement in EARS form has its trigger, condition, and response as separate, identifiable parts — exactly what's needed to tag it under FURPS+ and to compare it against others in a conflict-detection grid. entries.title: Requirements Engineering - Lecture Slides ver 1.1.pdf · p. 38
entries.text: 4.5.2 ORGANIZING REQUIREMENTS User Requirements vs. System Requirements User Requirements System Requirements Written for Stakeholders (non-technical) Developers and testers Style Natural language, simple tables, diagrams Structured, technical, precise What services does the user need? What are What exact functions, API endpoints, data Answers the business goals? structures, and constraints must exist? Why this distinction matters. User Requirements keep the SRS in language every stakeholder can validate and sign off on; System Requirements give developers and testers the precision to build and verify. Blur the two and either stakeholders can't confirm you understood them, or developers are left guessing — which is exactly how the “rabbit hole” trap (next slide) happens. Chapter 4 — Requirements Engineering 39

entries.title: Requirements Engineering - Lecture Slides ver 1.1.pdf · p. 39
entries.text: 4.5.2 ORGANIZING REQUIREMENTS Avoid the “Rabbit Hole” Trap Novice engineers often dive into low-level System Requirements — database schemas, API protocols, caching — before fully understanding the high-level User Requirements. This builds a well-engineered system that solves the wrong problem. Rule of thumb: you cannot specify how a system should work until you fully understand what problem the user is trying to solve. Chapter 4 — Requirements Engineering 40

entries.title: Requirements Engineering - Lecture Slides ver 1.1.pdf · p. 40
entries.text: 4.5.2 EXAMPLE Example User Requirement to System Requirement Question to Ask. To write user requirement into system requirement, engineer must ask the following questions: - • Hardware requirement: Which mobile device platforms is supporting? • Data requirement: What class schedule related content should be displayed? • Performance, reliability, security, etc. ? UR-001.1: The system shall display the student's class schedule on mobile devices as well as on desktop portal SR-001.1: The system shall render the class schedule page on iOS 17 or later (Safari) and Android 13 or later (Chrome) SR-001.2: The class schedule page shall display, for each class, the course code, course name, day, start time, end time, room, and instructor SR-001.3: The class schedule shown on a mobile device shall contain the same entries as the class schedule shown on the desktop portal for the same student and term SR-001.4: The student portal shall require the student to be authenticated before displaying the class schedule on any device Chapter 4 — Requirements Engineering 23

entries.title: Requirements Engineering - Lecture Slides ver 1.1.pdf · p. 41
entries.text: 4.5.2 ORGANIZING REQUIREMENTS Viewpoint-Oriented Analysis (VOA) Purpose: VOA groups requirements by the perspective they come from, so analysis works through each perspective in turn instead of one undifferentiated pile: INTERACTOR INDIRECT DOMAIN Direct Users Indirect Stakeholders Domain Constraints People who directly interact with Never touch the system, but rely Environmental and technical the UI. on its outputs (auditors, limits imposed by the domain executives). itself. Why we need it. Requirements gathered from only one viewpoint — usually Direct Users — systematically miss Indirect Stakeholders' needs and Domain Constraints, exactly the kind of gap that surfaces expensively during Validation, or worse, after deployment. Checking all three viewpoints before Specification is what makes the analysis complete, not just plausible. Chapter 4 — Requirements Engineering 41

entries.title: Requirements Engineering - Lecture Slides ver 1.1.pdf · p. 42
entries.text: 4.5.3 FR & NFR IN DEPTH Functional Requirements, by Category Functional Requirements (FR) define a specific behavior the system must perform. They answer “what does the system do?” and are written using the EARS patterns you learned in Section 4.5.1. Category Example Functional Requirement WHEN a student updates their profile address, the system shall update the central student Data Management information database. User Management The system shall allow an administrator to deactivate a lecturer account. Reporting The system shall generate a weekly room-utilization report grouped by department. WHEN a new semester is created, the system shall synchronize course codes with the Integration university's ERP system. Chapter 4 — Requirements Engineering 52

entries.text: 4.5.3 FR & NFR IN DEPTH Writing Measurable Non-Functional Requirements Non-Functional Requirements (NFR) define a quality attribute — not what the system does, but how well. An NFR is only useful if a tester can look at it and say Pass or Fail with no argument. Example: When a student opens the class schedule page over a 4G connection, the system shall display the schedule within 3 seconds The <system> shall <behavior> within/under <threshold + unit> when/under <condition>. Metric Threshold Condition What is being measured (time, A specific number with a unit. The context under which the throughput, error rate, uptime %, “Fast” is not a threshold; “2 threshold applies (load level, concurrent users). seconds” is. network type, hardware). entries.text: 4.5.3 CHALLENGE: FR VS. NFR BLENDING Resolution — the FURPS+ Framework Stakeholders rarely separate the two on their own. Engineers are expected to identify FR apart from NFR. — FURPS+ gives six categories to sort them into: F Functionality U Usability R Reliability Features, capabilities, Human factors, Availability, accuracy, security aesthetics, docs recoverability P Performance S Supportability + Constraints Speed, throughput, Testability, maintainability Design, Implementation, response time Interface, Physical Example: “The system shall print invoices instantly” splits into a Functional req. (support printing) + a Performance req. (completes within 2 seconds). Chapter 4 — Requirements Engineering 42

entries.title: Requirements Engineering - Lecture Slides ver 1.1.pdf · p. 47
entries.text: 4.5.3 FREQUENTLY ASKED Is the “F” in FURPS+ the Same as a Functional Requirement (FR)? No —It is not a true Functional Requirement. ”F” in FURPS+ (Functionality) is a category — feature set, security scope, audit and compliance controls — used to group and review related requirements together. It is a label, not a testable sentence. FR (Functional Requirement) is one individual, EARS-formatted, testable statement (Section 4.6.3) Why put an F in an NFR-style framework? They describe a quality of a function, not the function itself. But got grouped under "F" because they don't fit neatly under Usability, Reliability, Performance, or Supportability either. Chapter 4 — Requirements Engineering 43

entries.text: THE SIMPLE TEST One Question Separates Them Can I remove this requirement and the system still does the same task, just less safely, traceably, or controllably? NO — THE TASK DISAPPEARS YES — THE TASK STILL WORKS → It’s a true FR → It sits under “F” Write it as an EARS statement and attach it Document it once as a cross-cutting review item, directly to the feature's acceptance criteria. referenced by every feature it touches. Example: “The system shall allow a user to cancel Example: “All trading actions require MFA” or a pending order before execution.” “every trade generates an immutable audit log entry.” FURPS+ Quick Reference — FR vs. “F” 3

A Working Example Requirement Type Why The system shall allow a user to place a limit order FR Removing it deletes a feature. specifying price and quantity. The system shall allow a user to cancel a pending order FR A discrete, testable action. before execution. Order placement still works — just The system shall encrypt all API traffic using TLS 1.2+. “F” insecurely — without it. Score every pair: +1 Compatible, 0 Neutral, −1 Conflict. FR1: Mobile NFR1: Load < 3s NFR2: Encryption FR2: Swap FR1: Mobile — +1 0 0 NFR1: Load < 3s +1 — −1 (Conflict) 0 NFR2: Encryption 0 −1 (Conflict) — 0 FR2: Swap 0 0 0 — Reading it: NFR1 and NFR2 conflict — encryption overhead works against the load-time budget, an explicit trade-off is needed before any code is written. From Organized Requirements to a Baselined SRS Requirements Specification takes the organized, classified requirements from Phase 2 and writes them into one authoritative, contractually-binding document: the Software Requirements Specification (SRS). entries.text: 4.8.1 TRACEABILITY Forward, Backward, and Bidirectional Type Direction Purpose Connects user requirements down to specs, code, and tests — Bidirectional Both ways and back. Every requirement is designed, coded, tested. Prevents “omitted Forward Requirement → Code/Test scope.” Every piece of code maps to an authorized requirement. Prevents Backward Code/Test → Requirement “Gold Plating.” What is “Gold Plating”? Building unrequested features or unnecessary complexity — “while I'm in here, I'll also add…” It inflates cost and schedule without adding contracted value. Backward traceability is the main defense: if code doesn't map to a requirement ID, it shouldn't exist. Chapter 4 — Requirements Engineering 65

entries.text: CASE STUDY CHECKPOINT Traceability & Change Control: A Real ECR Six months after baselining, a new data-privacy regulation requires all schedule data in transit to be encrypted end-to-end — the risk the Interaction Grid had only flagged as “future” back in Analysis. A Facility IT lead submits an ECR. The ECR writes the anticipated risk into a real requirement for the first time: NFR2 — “The system shall encrypt all schedule and swap-request data in transit using TLS 1.3, and at rest using AES-256.” The team consults the RTM: the change touches SR-1.1 and its test case TC-API-204 will need updating, since encryption overhead affects the 3.0s load-time budget — precisely the NFR1-vs-NFR2 trade-off logged during Analysis. The CCB approves it — the SRS is re-baselined as v1.1, and the RTM rows for SR-1.1 and the new NFR2 are updated. Chapter 4 — Requirements Engineering 71

entries.text: QUICK REFERENCE Telling the ID Codes Apart Several ID prefixes appear side by side in this chapter — here's how to tell them apart: Prefix Meaning Assigned During Example E-xxx Raw statement from Elicitation, unanalyzed. Phase 1 (Elicitation) E-002 UC-xx Use Case: an actor–system interaction. Phase 1 → Phase 3 UC-04 UR-x User Requirement — organized, for stakeholders. Phase 2 (Analysis) UR-2 SR-x.x System Requirement — technical, from one UR. Phase 3 (Specification) SR-2.1 FRx / NFRx Functional / Non-Functional Requirement (SRS's list). Phase 3 (Specification) FR1, NFR1 TC-xxx Test Case — verifies one requirement (in the RTM). Phase 4 (Validation) TC-API-204 Reading the numbering. SR-2.1 means “the 1st System Requirement derived from UR-2” — the decimal ties it to its parent UR. FR/NFR numbers, by contrast, just count sequentially through the SRS's formal requirement list; they don't encode a parent ID. Chapter 4 — Requirements Engineering 73

entries.title: Reparar al nieto interior
entries.text: Inserte 30, 10, 20 en un árbol AVL vacío. La raíz es 30; su hijo izquierdo es 10, cuyo hijo derecho es 20. Las alturas cuentan las aristas. ¿Qué reparación preserva el orden BST y restablece el equilibrio? El nieto interior debe convertirse primero en el niño exterior. Gire a la izquierda en 10, luego a la derecha en 30: la raíz de 20 tiene hijos 10 y 30. Solo gira a la izquierda en 30 Trampa: alejarse del pesado subárbol no puede reparar esta forma. Intercambia las claves 10 y 30 sin cambiar los enlaces. Trampa: el equilibrio es estructural; El intercambio de claves puede interrumpir el recorrido ordenado. Rotación a la izquierda en 10, luego rotación a la derecha en 30 Correcto: este es el caso izquierda-derecha, no el caso izquierda-izquierda. Solo gira a la derecha en 30 Trampa: usar la reparación izquierda-izquierda para una inserción interna deja un desequilibrio diferente.

entries.title: Los límites de altura no comparan una carga de trabajo
entries.text: Un servicio utiliza un árbol AVL. Otro equipo propone un árbol rojo-negro para una carga de trabajo mixta de búsqueda/inserción/eliminación. No se han recopilado puntos de referencia. ¿Qué conclusión es defendible? Ambos mantienen una altura logarítmica. Diferentes invariantes de equilibrio afectan las constantes y actualizan el trabajo; la implementación más rápida depende de la carga de trabajo y el comportamiento de la memoria. Un límite de altura por sí solo no establece la velocidad del reloj de pared. Los árboles rojo-negro tienen búsqueda en el peor de los casos O (1) Trampa: el equilibrio más débil sigue siendo logarítmico, no de profundidad constante. AVL siempre gana porque está más equilibrado Trampa: menor altura no representa costos de mantenimiento e implementación. La eliminación de AVL requiere como máximo una reparación en un ancestro Trampa: la eliminación puede propagar los cambios de altura hacia la raíz. Ambos tienen búsqueda O (log n); costos de búsqueda y actualización de puntos de referencia Correcto: las garantías asintóticas no seleccionan una implementación universalmente más rápida.

entries.title: Un vértice finalizado se vuelve más barato
entries.text: Bordes dirigidos: s→a cuesta 2, s→b cuesta 5, b→a cuesta −4. No hay otros bordes. Dijkstra se instala permanentemente a antes de b. ¿Qué diagnóstico es correcto? El camino s→b→a cuesta 1, pero a se resolvió con una distancia 2. Un borde negativo invalida el argumento de finalización habitual incluso sin un ciclo negativo. Bellman-Ford admite pesos negativos cuando ningún ciclo negativo alcanzable impide caminos más cortos finitos. Es seguro porque no hay ciclo negativo. Trampa: la ausencia de ciclos negativos es insuficiente para el estándar Dijkstra. Agregue 4 a cada borde y use el mismo camino más corto Trampa: las rutas con diferentes recuentos de bordes reciben diferentes compensaciones totales. La distancia más corta a a es 2 porque su borde directo es el más pequeño Trampa: la elección del borde local no es una prueba de la optimización del camino más corto. Dijkstra puede finalizar la distancia equivocada; utilizar un algoritmo de peso negativo adecuado Correcto: un recorrido posterior mejora un vértice ya asentado.

entries.title: La representación es parte del encuadernación.
entries.text: Gráfico no negativo. La versión A utiliza listas de adyacencia y un montón binario. La versión B escanea una matriz de distancias para cada mínimo y utiliza una matriz de adyacencia. ¿Qué límite estándar se ajusta a estas implementaciones? El recorrido de la lista toca los bordes O(E); Las operaciones de montón contribuyen con una sobrecarga logarítmica, lo que produce O((V+E) log V). Los escaneos mínimos de la matriz y las filas de la matriz producen O (V²) en la implementación densa estándar. Ambos: O(E log E), independientemente de la representación Trampa: los escaneos matriciales pueden visitar entradas en busca de bordes ausentes. A: O(V); B: O(E) Trampa: ninguno de los dos tiene cuentas para seleccionar el siguiente mínimo. A: O(V²); B: O(log V) Trampa: el límite del montón se asigna a la implementación de la matriz y el trabajo total logarítmico ni siquiera puede leer este gráfico. A: O((V+E)log V); B: O(V²) Correcto: tanto la cola de prioridad como la representación de adyacencia son importantes.

entries.title: La densidad no es una prueba 0/1
entries.text: Capacidad 50. Artículos (peso,valor): (10,60), (20,100), (30,120). Un algoritmo ávido de densidad toma los dos primeros. Los artículos no se pueden dividir. ¿Qué resultado y justificación son válidos? El valor elegido es 160; tomando los artículos de peso 20 y peso 30 se obtiene 220. La selección de densidad funciona para mochila fraccionaria porque se permite el intercambio de fracciones; Los elementos indivisibles eliminan ese argumento. Codicioso obtiene 160; el optimo es 220 Correcto: este pequeño contraejemplo refuta la optimización universal de la densidad ávida de mochila 0/1. Codicioso es óptimo en 160 porque la densidad es más alta Trampa: importar el argumento fraccionario de elección codiciosa al problema indivisible. Llévate los tres por 280 Trampa: los pesos suman 60 y violan la restricción de capacidad. Toma la mitad del último artículo para llegar a 220. Trampa: cambiar el problema a mochila fraccionada viola las reglas establecidas.

entries.title: Una clave de memorización pierde una decisión.
entries.text: Un solucionador de mochila 0/1 (i, capacidad restante) decide si se toma el elemento i y luego avanza a i+1. Un programador almacena en caché solo la capacidad restante. ¿Por qué esto puede arrojar un resultado incorrecto? Dos subproblemas con la misma capacidad pueden tener elementos restantes diferentes. La caché debe conservar todos los componentes de estado necesarios para determinar opciones futuras, como (i, capacidad). La superposición de subproblemas por sí sola no hace que un estado incompleto sea válido. La clave omite qué elementos quedan; incluirme Correcto: capacidades iguales no implican opciones factibles iguales. La memorización requiere almacenar el seguimiento completo de la ejecución anterior. Trampa: el requisito es un estado suficiente, no un historial completo. La programación dinámica no puede resolver la mochila 0/1 Trampa: la recurrencia estándar de artículo/capacidad es válida; su coste pseudopolinomial es un tema aparte. Mantenga siempre el valor en caché más grande en i Trampa: ese valor puede usar un elemento no disponible en el subproblema actual.

entries.title: Un agregado lento, muchos agregados baratos
entries.text: Una matriz dinámica inicialmente vacía duplica su capacidad cuando está llena; cada anexo escribe un elemento. Analice N anexos sin encogimiento. ¿Qué afirmación es correcta? Las copias se producen a capacidades geométricamente crecientes. Su suma es O(N), por lo que el trabajo total es O(N) y el apéndice amortizado es O(1). Un anexo de cambio de tamaño individual todavía puede costar O(N). O(1) anexo amortizado, con O(N) anexo de cambio de tamaño en el peor de los casos Correcto: un límite de secuencia no elimina operaciones individuales costosas. Cada anexo tiene O(1) trabajo en el peor de los casos Trampa: copiar todos los elementos existentes es un verdadero trabajo. La secuencia cuesta O(N²) porque un anexo es lineal Trampa: multiplicar el máximo por cada operación ignora la poca frecuencia con la que se producen cambios de tamaño. Amortizado significa promedio sobre entradas aleatorias Trampa: el análisis amortizado limita una secuencia de operaciones sin requerir una distribución de probabilidad de entrada.

entries.title: Casi constante no es literalmente constante
entries.text: Un bosque de conjunto disjunto combina unión por rango con compresión de ruta sobre una secuencia de uniones y hallazgos. ¿Qué describe el resultado habitual de Ackermann inverso? Las heurísticas combinadas dan un costo de operación amortizado de Ackermann inverso sobre una secuencia, a menudo tratado como casi constante para tamaños prácticos. No es un límite literal O(1) en el peor de los casos para cada búsqueda, y el rango almacenado no necesita ser igual a la altura actual después de la compresión. El rango por sí solo demuestra el resultado inverso de Ackermann Trampa: el límite combinado más fuerte depende de la compresión y del enlace equilibrado. O(α(n)) costo amortizado; los hallazgos individuales no tienen por qué ser constantes Correcto: distinguir el comportamiento de secuencia de una garantía del peor de los casos por llamada. Cada hallazgo sigue exactamente un puntero. Trampa: la compresión beneficia llamadas posteriores; una ruta sin comprimir puede tener varios bordes. La compresión de ruta mantiene el rango igual a la altura actual exacta Trampa: los rangos se mantienen para vincular decisiones y no se vuelven a calcular después de la compresión.

entries.title: El subtipo fortalece el contrato.
entries.text: Account.withdraw(x) promete aceptar cualquier saldo 0 ≤ x ≤. Una subclase de FixedTermAccount se lanza por cada retiro antes del vencimiento, incluso cuando se cumple la condición previa base. ¿Qué rediseño respeta a los clientes de la abstracción base? El subtipo impone una condición previa adicional, rompiendo el comportamiento prometido por los clientes de la Cuenta. Una interfaz con capacidad de retiro puede representar esa capacidad; un producto de duración determinada puede compartir el almacenamiento a través de la composición sin reclamar un retiro irrestricto. Cambie el nombre del método de subclase y mantenga el mismo contrato de cuenta Trampa: el cambio de nombre no puede satisfacer el comportamiento que todavía se promete a los clientes. Capacidad de retiro dividido y implementación compartida a través de la composición Correcto: la reutilización debe preservar la promesa de comportamiento de la interfaz anunciada. Mantener la herencia porque ambas clases tienen un campo de equilibrio. Trampa: la coincidencia de campos de datos no establece una sustituibilidad de comportamiento. Detecte todas las excepciones en todos los sitios de llamadas de cuentas existentes Trampa: esto cambia las suposiciones del cliente en lugar de respetar la abstracción original.

entries.title: Una secuencia de inicio no es una responsabilidad
entries.text: StartupManager valida facturas, borra cachés de imágenes y envía recordatorios porque todo se ejecuta a las 08:00. Los cambios en la política de facturación requieren editar esta misma clase. ¿Qué juicio describe mejor la agrupación? Un tiempo de ejecución compartido es una evidencia débil de unidad funcional. Separar las operaciones de dominio y componerlas en un programador mantiene la orquestación explícita. Una división automática de microservicios agregaría costos operativos distribuidos sin demostrar una necesidad de implementación. Agrupación temporal; Separe las responsabilidades y mantenga un programador explícito. Correcto: organice el comportamiento del dominio en torno a los motivos para cambiar manteniendo la orquestación necesaria. Alta cohesión funcional porque cada tarea se ejecuta a las 08:00 Trampa: se confunde el tiempo de ejecución con una responsabilidad de dominio compartida. Crear tres servicios de red únicamente para mejorar la cohesión. Trampa: la distribución de procesos no mejora por sí sola los límites de los módulos. Coloque cada operación en un singleton de utilidad para reducir el acoplamiento. Trampa: un punto de acceso global compartido puede ocultar dependencias en lugar de eliminarlas.

entries.title: Un límite de API agrega modos de falla
entries.text: Un equipo de cuatro personas posee una pequeña aplicación cuyos módulos ya tienen interfaces claras. No existe ningún requisito de implementación o escalamiento independiente. ¿Cuál próximo paso cuenta con el mayor apoyo? Mantenga los límites del módulo y mida las restricciones de implementación o escalamiento reales antes de introducir llamadas remotas. Los servicios en red añaden fallas parciales, latencia y operaciones; un único sistema desplegable aún puede ser modular. Mantenga un monolito modular y vuelva a visitarlo cuando las necesidades operativas justifiquen la división. Correcto: la distribución debería resolver una restricción evidenciada. Los microservicios garantizan un bajo acoplamiento Trampa: los servicios pueden permanecer estrechamente coordinados a través de esquemas compartidos y supuestos de implementación. Un monolito no puede tener alta cohesión Trampa: no es lo mismo una unidad de despliegue que un módulo o responsabilidad. Dividir primero; la integración y el seguimiento se pueden aplazar indefinidamente Trampa: los límites remotos introducen fallas inmediatamente, no sólo después de que el equipo crece.

entries.title: Una instancia no es una solicitud
entries.text: Un RequestContext singleton almacena el usuario actual. Las solicitudes A y B configuran simultáneamente el usuario actual y luego calculan una decisión de autorización. ¿Cuál es el defecto central? Un singleton comparte el mismo campo de solicitud mutable. El entrelazado puede sobrescribir la identidad de una solicitud con la de otra. Pasar datos inmutables del ámbito de la solicitud a la operación de autorización; La construcción singleton segura por sí sola no hace que todas las operaciones posteriores sean seguras. El bloqueo de inicialización singleton evita todas las carreras posteriores Trampa: la publicación del objeto y la sincronización de sus operaciones mutables son cuestiones diferentes. Marcar usuario actual como público para que todos los hilos estén de acuerdo con su valor. Trampa: los modificadores de visibilidad no proporcionan aislamiento de solicitudes. Agregue un segundo singleton a solicitudes alternativas Trampa: un número fijo de espacios compartidos no puede representar de forma segura solicitudes simultáneas arbitrarias. Estado de solicitud mutable compartido; pasar un contexto de solicitud explícito Correcto: la vida útil y el aislamiento deben coincidir con los datos.

entries.title: Una fábrica más grande que sus necesidades.
entries.text: Una calculadora de precios debe elegir entre dos reglas de descuento sin estado. No existe una familia de productos relacionados ni un ciclo de vida mutable. ¿Qué diseño se ajusta a la necesidad declarada? Una función inyectada o una pequeña interfaz de estrategia hace que la variación sea explícita. Abstract Factory está destinado a la creación de productos relacionados; agregarlo aquí introduce maquinaria sin un requisito demostrado. Revise la elección si la variación crece. Duplica toda la calculadora para cada descuento Trampa: variar una regla no debería duplicar un comportamiento de cálculo no relacionado. Inyectar una función o estrategia de descuento Correcto: aísle la variación real con una pequeña dependencia explícita. Cree una jerarquía de Abstract Factory para cada posible descuento futuro Trampa: las familias de productos especulativas aumentan la complejidad antes de que exista el requisito. Utilice un singleton cuyo modo cambie antes de cada llamada. Trampa: la selección mutable global introduce ordenamiento oculto y dependencias de concurrencia.

entries.title: Mocks verdes, formato de cable roto.
entries.text: Una prueba de servicio se burla de un cliente de pago para obtener éxito. Producción rechaza solicitudes porque el campo de moneda serializada usa un nombre incorrecto. Todas las pruebas aisladas pasan. ¿Qué control específico falta? Una prueba que ejercite la serialización real y el contrato API puede detectar una discrepancia que un simulacro pasa por alto. Mantenga pruebas unitarias rápidas para decisiones locales; agregue una prueba de límites enfocada y un pequeño flujo de un extremo a otro en lugar de asumir que cualquiera de las capas por sí sola cubre todo. Vuelva a intentar los pagos de producción fallidos hasta que pase una prueba Trampa: los reintentos no reparan errores de contrato deterministas y pueden repetir efectos secundarios. Una verificación real de serialización/integración de contratos en el límite de pago Correcto: verifique el comportamiento que reemplazó el simulacro. Más afirmaciones sobre la misma respuesta de éxito simulada Trampa: la prueba aún no puede observar el formato real del cable. Reemplace cada prueba unitaria con automatización de la interfaz de usuario Trampa: las pruebas lentas y amplias descartan un aislamiento útil y hacen que las fallas sean más difíciles de localizar.

entries.title: Un sueño oculta la condición de sincronización.
entries.text: Una prueba inicia un trabajo en segundo plano, duerme 100 ms y luego afirma que se ha completado. Pasa localmente pero falla bajo carga de CI. ¿Qué reparación aborda mejor la causa? Espere a que se cumpla la condición de finalización observable con un tiempo de espera limitado o controle el programador/reloj en una prueba aislada. La duración fija del sueño adivina la velocidad de programación; una espera ilimitada ocultaría un trabajo estancado. Aumentar el sueño a diez segundos para cada prueba. Trampa: las esperas más largas siguen siendo conjeturas de tiempo y ralentizan la suite. Ignorar errores después de un reintento exitoso Trampa: la repetición oculta la inestabilidad sin arreglar el contrato de sincronización. Eliminar la afirmación de finalización Trampa: eliminar el cheque elimina la evidencia de que el trabajo funciona. Espere una señal de finalización con un tiempo de espera limitado Correcto: sincronice el comportamiento en lugar de adivinar el tiempo transcurrido.

entries.title: Cuando las coincidencias correctas agotan la CPU
entries.text: Incidente documentado: el 2 de julio de 2019, una regla WAF de Cloudflare provocó el agotamiento de la CPU debido al retroceso de expresiones regulares. Su conjunto de pruebas no identificó un consumo excesivo de CPU. Las siguientes opciones de prevención son un ejercicio didáctico original. ¿Qué control apunta a la brecha reportada? Los ejemplos de coincidencias funcionales por sí solos no vinculan el uso de recursos. Pruebe coincidencias adversas con presupuestos de recursos explícitos y revise la complejidad del motor; una implementación basada en autómatas puede evitar un retroceso catastrófico para las expresiones regulares admitidas. Supongamos que una expresión regular sintácticamente válida tiene un tiempo de ejecución lineal Trampa: el reconocimiento del lenguaje y la estrategia de ejecución del motor elegido son diferentes. Aumente la memoria del servidor sin probar la ejecución de expresiones regulares Trampa: el cuello de botella informado fue el agotamiento de la CPU, no evidencia de memoria insuficiente. Pruebe coincidencias adversas con un presupuesto de CPU/tiempo Correcto: mide el modo de falla reportado en el incidente. Agregue solo ejemplos de coincidencia más normales Trampa: los caminos felices representativos pueden pasar por alto el retroceso patológico.

entries.title: Una copia de seguridad es útil sólo si restaura
entries.text: Incidente documentado: la interrupción de la base de datos de GitLab en enero de 2017 expuso rutas de respaldo/recuperación poco confiables. Su autopsia describe las fallas de pg_dump y la recuperación de una copia de seguridad provisional creada manualmente. Las opciones siguientes son un ejercicio de prevención original. ¿Qué prueba valida mejor el contrato de recuperación? Un trabajo de respaldo que informa el éxito no puede establecer la capacidad de recuperación. La restauración periódica en un entorno aislado pone en práctica las herramientas, las versiones y los datos almacenados reales. Verificar los datos recuperados y alertar sobre fallas tanto en la copia de seguridad como en la restauración; Mantenga los datos de producción seguros durante los simulacros. Comprobando solo que existe un nombre de archivo de respaldo Trampa: un archivo puede existir sin contener datos de recuperación utilizables. Tratar la replicación sola como una copia de seguridad independiente probada Trampa: la replicación y la recuperabilidad son garantías separadas; Los cambios destructivos pueden propagarse. Un simulacro de restauración aislado con afirmaciones de datos recuperados y alertas de fallas Correcto: esto ejercita el comportamiento de recuperación en lugar de solo la interfaz de comando de respaldo. Un cliente de respaldo simulado que siempre arroja éxito Trampa: un doble aislado pasa por alto el límite de recuperación que falló.
